chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
title: Why musicians used hard drugs
summary: Collins says drugs had nothing to do with music and were an escape from social conditions, with young players imitating Charlie Parker.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: What relationship, really, do you think it has to music?
Not any as far as I can see.
Why do those musicians, you think, I mean (inaudible).
Well, I'll tell you. You know, it's -- I think it really was an escape, because of the frustrating social conditions, not being able to work here, or certain places you just couldn't work, you know.
Did anybody do you think really feel that it made them more expressive or --
(inaudible) their music. Would anybody want to do it for that reason?
Well, I'll tell you what. There are followers, you know, some people are born followers, and

say like Charlie Parker, it was commonly known that he used dope. So naturally some impressionable young musician assumed that it would make them play better if it worked for Bird -- Bird, it would work for them. Which was not true, you know. So I think this was how it really got kind of out of hand.
But no, I don't think it contributed anything, as a matter of fact.
